name: nlgeom-cantilever-hex20
reference: Benchmark K2, the large-deflection cantilever, against the exact Euler elastica. A 1 m x 5 mm x 5 mm steel cantilever (L/h = 200), 20 hex20 elements, carries a fixed-direction transverse tip force of 15.084505 N, which is alpha = PL^2/EI = 1.3791547. The reference is not a published table: `the_large_deflection_cantilever_follows_the_elastica` in crates/engine/tests/fem.rs derives it by quadrature of the elastica's own first integral. With EI theta'' = -P cos theta, theta(0) = 0 and theta'(L) = 0, the first integral is theta' = sqrt(2P/EI) sqrt(sin theta_L - sin theta), so for a chosen tip slope theta_L the load parameter and the tip position are three integrals of one integrand; theta_L = 0.6 rad gives alpha = 1.3791547, x_tip = 0.90488893 L and y_tip = 0.38725775 L, and at small alpha the same quadrature reduces to theta_L = alpha/2 and y = alpha L/3, which is Euler-Bernoulli. Measured: -382.17 mm across against -387.26 mm, 1.31 %. Refining to 40 elements gives -385.27 mm (0.49 %), so the gap is the mesh and not the formulation; the gate is 2 % at 20 elements, which keeps the case fast. Linear theory would say PL^3/3EI = -459.72 mm, so the geometric stiffening this case measures is 16 % - it is not a rounding correction, and a linear Step gets it wrong by more than a quarter. Bisshopp & Drucker (1945) tabulate the same curve; their published values are **resolve** until the paper is on hand, and nothing here depends on them.

checks.note: tip deflection in mm, within 2 % of the exact elastica at alpha = 1.3791547
and the tip draws in by L - x_tip, which only a finite-deformation kinematics produces at all
A7: the reactions balance the applied load at the converged state
